node-1.label: A 7-year-old boy presented with behavioral issues since infancy.

node-2.label: Early developmental history: first child, unplanned pregnancy, oligohydramnios at 36 weeks, possible congenital cardiac defects noted in fetus; delivered preterm at 36 weeks via emergency cesarean section due to fetal bradycardia; birth weight 1.7 kg, delayed cry, and cyanosed at birth; cardiac evaluation at birth identified patent ductus arteriosus, ventricular septal defect, tricuspid regurgitation, and a left atrium to right atrium shunt, and he was started on digitoxin.

node-3.label: As he grew, he exhibited global developmental delay and was diagnosed with bilateral profound sensorineural hearing loss at 6 months of age; over time he continued to show delayed milestones and developed poor eye contact, poor social and communication skills, repetitive head rocking, hand flapping movements, and a preference for fixed routines.

node-4.label: From the age of 3, he displayed symptoms of attention deficit hyperkinetic disorder (ADHD), including an inability to sit still for more than 2-3 minutes and difficulty engaging in activities; his insistence on routine and hyperactivity increased over the years, leading to aggressive behaviors such as hitting and biting his mother, which resulted in significant distress and a psychiatry consultation with subsequent admission to a child psychiatry inpatient unit; there was no history of head injury, seizures, frequent diarrhea and vomiting, birthmarks, or failure to thrive.

node-5.label: Physical examination revealed a small head circumference (49 cm) and bilateral flat feet; mental status examination showed a lack of eye contact, hyperactivity, irritable mood, frequent side-to-side head movements, and hand flapping; his intelligence quotient was evaluated to be 25.

attrs.why: Poor eye contact, repetitive head rocking, hand flapping, routine insistence, aggression, microcephaly, flat feet, and IQ 25 continue to be best explained by autism with profound intellectual disability. Both the laboratory physician and radiologist independently affirm this phenotype, and the newly reported MRI and ophthalmologic findings reflect the underlying etiologic process rather than altering the autism diagnosis, so confidence is held at 0.85.

New expert data: brain MRI shows multifocal symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensities and ophthalmology reveals pigmentary retinopathy, a pattern the radiologist and laboratory physician both consider suggestive of a genetic/metabolic syndrome. Combined with congenital cardiac defects, preterm birth, global delay, hearing loss, and microcephaly, this unifying pattern raises confidence in a genetic syndromic disorder from 0.70 to 0.75.

Multifocal symmetric white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensities and pigmentary retinopathy can also occur in congenital infection, and the experts note that congenital infection cannot be excluded because genetic/TORCH testing is unavailable. However, the absence of failure to thrive and birthmarks keeps it less likely than a genetic cause, so confidence rises only modestly from 0.40 to 0.45.

node-12.label: Genetic/metabolic disorder with retinal and white matter involvement (possible leukodystrophy)

attrs.why: The combination of symmetric white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensities and pigmentary retinopathy in a child with global delay, hearing loss, microcephaly, and congenital cardiac defects suggests a genetic/metabolic disorder involving both retina and white matter (such as a leukodystrophy or related metabolic syndrome), which could unify the autism/profound-ID phenotype and the systemic findings. Confidence is moderate pending genetic/metabolic testing.

node-13.label: The patient exhibits the classic congenital rubella triad: sensorineural hearing loss, pigmentary retinopathy, and patent ductus arteriosus

attrs.why: The patient's combination of profound sensorineural hearing loss, pigmentary retinopathy, and congenital cardiac defects including patent ductus arteriosus and ventricular septal defect matches the classic triad of congenital rubella syndrome, accompanied by microcephaly and global developmental delay. Because the experts note that congenital infection cannot be excluded while TORCH testing is unavailable, and the cardiac, auditory and ocular features co-occur in a syndrome-typical pattern, a specific congenital rubella etiology is proposed with moderate confidence, though it remains unconfirmed.
